title: A Physics-Informed Fourier-Wavelet Transformer for Multiscale Computational Fluid Dynamics Surrogate Modeling
authors: Somyajit Chakraborty, Ming Pan, Xizhong Chen
abstract: Physics-informed surrogate models can accelerate computational fluid dynamics simulations. However, many existing methods reproduce global flow patterns more reliably than localized multiscale structures. This study presents a physics-informed Fourier-wavelet transformer for next-step velocity-field reconstruction in real-world flow benchmarks. The proposed formulation combines hybrid Fourier-wavelet spectral encoding with physics-biased self-attention based on partial differential equation residual diagnostics. It also uses self-supervised pretraining through Masked Physics Prediction and Equation Consistency Prediction. The experiments are conducted on two real benchmark cases: cylinder-wake flow and fluid-structure interaction. All approaches are evaluated under a shared local protocol and compared with spectral, transformer-based, operator-learning, and physics-informed neural-network baselines. On the cylinder-wake benchmark, the proposed model achieves the best aggregate accuracy, with an all-channel normalized mean-squared error of 0.05875 and an all-channel Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.97019. On the fluid-structure-interaction benchmark, it gives the lowest all-channel normalized mean-squared error of $2.70 \times 10^{-4}$, compared with $4.02 \times 10^{-4}$ for the strongest baseline. Component-wise field comparisons and scale-separated diagnostics further show stronger recovery of localized wake structures, including near-body, wake-core, and far-wake features. The results demonstrate improved real-world flow reconstruction while maintaining a practical accuracy-cost tradeoff.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed Fourier-wavelet transformer improves multiscale CFD surrogate forecasting by combining spectral encoding, PDE-aware attention, and self-supervised physics pretraining to better recover localized flow structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a practical surrogate modeling route for accelerating real-world CFD and fluid-structure interaction simulations while preserving accuracy on both global and local flow features.
method: Hybrid Fourier-wavelet spectral encoding for multiscale flow representation
Physics-biased self-attention guided by PDE residual diagnostics
Self-supervised pretraining with Masked Physics Prediction and Equation Consistency Prediction
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on cylinder-wake and fluid-structure-interaction benchmarks, the model achieved best overall performance, including 0.05875 all-channel NMSE and 0.97019 PCC on cylinder wake, and 2.70×10^-4 all-channel NMSE on FSI versus 4.02×10^-4 for the strongest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is reported under a shared local benchmark protocol, so generalization to higher Reynolds numbers, different geometries, or longer rollout horizons still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: A Physics-Informed Fourier-Wavelet Transformer for Multiscale Computational Fluid Dynamics Surrogate Modeling

title: Data-Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
authors: Abed Hammoud, Edriss S. Titi Mitchell Bushuk, Marc Calaf, Khaled Ghannam, Elie Bou-Zeid
abstract: Turbulent fluxes in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) govern exchanges of momentum, heat, and mass between the surface and atmosphere, shaping boundary layer structure and influencing weather, climate, and engineering applications. Yet their representation in coarse resolution models remains challenging, particularly under unstable conditions with strongly nonlocal transport and stable conditions with intermittent turbulence. Here, we develop a data driven turbulent flux parameterization in which nondimensional fluxes are represented by a linearized convolution operator acting on nondimensional mean state profiles. We train and evaluate the closure using high resolution large eddy simulations (LES) of idealized flow over homogeneous surfaces spanning multiple stability regimes. Several first order closure variants are constructed from different combinations of mean temperature and velocity profiles to predict heat and momentum fluxes, and the best model is selected by minimizing mean squared error across training and unseen test cases. The resulting parameterization improves predictive skill relative to a standard K-profile closure while retaining an interpretable operator form. Its learned kernels expose the locality and nonlocality of turbulent transport across stability regimes, linking empirical performance to physically inspectable flux--profile relationships. In a posteriori single column simulations, the closure remains stable and produces state profiles that closely match LES, demonstrating its potential as an accurate and transparent ABL flux parameterization.

infographic.key_insight: A learned convolution-based closure can predict atmospheric boundary-layer heat and momentum fluxes from mean profiles more accurately than a standard K-profile scheme while remaining physically interpretable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical path to improve coarse-resolution weather and climate models with a transparent flux parameterization that is better suited for both unstable and stable boundary-layer conditions.
method: Train linearized convolution operators on nondimensional mean temperature and velocity profiles from high-resolution LES.
Test multiple first-order closure variants for heat and momentum flux prediction across stability regimes.
Select the best model by mean-squared error and assess it in a posteriori single-column simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was trained and evaluated on LES cases spanning multiple stability regimes and was also tested in single-column simulations, where it stayed stable and matched LES profiles closely.
infographic.watch_item: Because the closure is trained on idealized homogeneous-surface LES, performance may degrade in more heterogeneous or strongly non-ideal real-world boundary layers.
infographic.paper_title: Data-Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer

title: Towards bridging the gap between data-driven and theoretical turbulence closures in stratified flows
authors: Laure Zanna, Pavel Perezhogin
abstract: Turbulence closure models are essential for solving the equations of motion in realistic systems, where fully resolving all relevant scales of motion is computationally infeasible. Developing turbulence closures remains one of the most challenging problems in fluid dynamics. Specifically, the Navier-Stokes equations, when filtered to isolate large-scale motions, introduce new terms representing the influence of subgrid-scale turbulent stresses. These terms, which can only be computed directly by resolving the turbulence itself, therefore lead to the closure problem: we must add new equations or introduce assumptions to relate the unresolved scales of motions to the resolved flow. Here we consider the closure problem for oceanic flows, i.e., stratified, Boussinesq, incompressible, in a rotating frame of reference. In particular, we focus on a closure for ocean mesoscale eddies, which have horizontal scales of 10-100km and are key to the redistribution of momentum, energy, and tracers in the ocean. In particular, mesoscale eddies can reinject energy and momentum into the large-scale flow through an inverse energy cascade. Here, we explore a range of theoretical and data-driven ocean mesoscale closures and examine their connections using analytical and data-driven methods. This note aims to bridge the gap between novel methods from artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning and theoretical fluid dynamics to address significant challenges in the physics of turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: The paper connects data-driven and theoretical turbulence closures for stratified ocean flows, aiming to better represent unresolved mesoscale eddies in coarse-resolution models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Improved closure models can make ocean simulations more accurate and computationally feasible for predicting momentum, energy, and tracer transport.
method: Compare theoretical and AI/data-driven mesoscale closure formulations
Use analytical and data-driven methods to identify relationships between closure approaches
Target stratified, rotating, Boussinesq ocean dynamics with subgrid-scale effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract indicates the authors examine a range of theoretical and data-driven closures and analyze their connections, rather than presenting a single standalone benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Bridging theory and ML may improve interpretability, but closure performance and generalization can depend strongly on flow regime and training data coverage.
infographic.paper_title: Towards bridging the gap between data-driven and theoretical turbulence closures in stratified flows

title: A high-fidelity numerical database for free-stream transition
authors: Louenas Zemmour, Xavier Gloerfelt, Paola Cinnella
abstract: The accurate prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition is critical for the design of aerodynamic and turbomachinery systems, yet widely used experimental benchmarks, such as the ERCOFTAC T3 series, lack the full-field, three-dimensional, and time-resolved data required for modern model development. To address these limitations, this study presents a high-fidelity numerical database of bypass transition in boundary layers, generated using wall-resolved implicit Large Eddy Simulations (iLES) to rigorously mimic the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate experiments. Computations are performed using a high-order compressible Navier-Stokes solver across multiple configurations, encompassing a range of freestream turbulence intensities and both zero and varying pressure gradients. The numerical results demonstrate satisfactory agreement with legacy experimental data for skin friction, mean velocity, and fluctuation profiles. Finally, the resulting database is utilized to evaluate the predictive capabilities of standard Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models (SA-BCM and $k-ω-γ$), revealing systemic flaws in predicting transition onset and length. This highlights the dataset's value as a foundational resource for the calibration, assessment, and development of next-generation, physics-informed machine learning transition closures.

infographic.key_insight: A wall-resolved iLES database can reproduce bypass transition physics in flat-plate boundary layers more faithfully than legacy benchmarks and exposes major weaknesses in standard RANS transition models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This dataset provides a high-fidelity reference for improving transition prediction in aerodynamic and turbomachinery design, especially for calibration of physics-informed and machine-learning closures.
method: High-order compressible Navier-Stokes solver with implicit LES
ERCOFTAC T3-like flat-plate configurations
Multiple freestream turbulence levels with zero and varying pressure gradients
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations show satisfactory agreement with experimental skin friction, mean velocity, and fluctuation profiles, while SA-BCM and k-ω-γ models systematically mispredict transition onset and length.
infographic.watch_item: The database is highly resolved and configuration-specific, so transferring conclusions to other geometries or less-resolved CFD setups may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: A high-fidelity numerical database for free-stream transition

title: Numerical comparison of energy- versus circulation-preserving stochastic vortex dynamics
authors: Sagy Ephrati, Darryl D. Holm
abstract: We compare two geometric stochastic frameworks for the two-dimensional Euler equations, being the circulation-preserving stochastic advection by Lie transport (SALT) and the energy-preserving stochastic forcing by Lie transport (SFLT) approaches. While preserving both circulation and energy is ideal, their simultaneous conservation restricts perturbations to a stochastic reparametrization of time. Consequently, a fundamental choice must be made between preserving structure or the kinetic energy. Analysis reveals that SALT is significantly more sensitive to high-frequency flow components, with noise effects scaling by $| \bk |^2$ relative to SFLT. This suggests that SALT acts as a localized perturbation sensitive to sharp gradients, while SFLT behaves as a more regularized global forcing. Numerical experiments on a traveling dipole, vortex merger, and forced-damped turbulence confirm that SALT introduces uncertainty localized near dynamically active vorticity gradients, whereas SFLT produces a more diffuse variance field spread across the domain. These results illustrate how the choice of geometric invariant fundamentally determines scale-sensitivity and spatial distribution of modeled uncertainty in vortex dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that choosing between circulation-preserving SALT and energy-preserving SFLT fundamentally changes how stochastic uncertainty enters 2D vortex dynamics: SALT is more sensitive to high-frequency gradients, while SFLT spreads forcing more smoothly.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For turbulence and CFD uncertainty modeling, the framework choice determines whether randomness is localized around sharp vorticity features or distributed as a broader, more regularized forcing.
method: Compared two geometric stochastic formulations for the 2D Euler equations: SALT and SFLT.
Analyzed how each model scales with flow frequency, showing SALT noise effects grow like |k|^2 relative to SFLT.
Tested both models on traveling dipole, vortex merger, and forced-damped turbulence cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments across three flow scenarios, consistently finding SALT variance concentrated near active vorticity gradients and SFLT variance spread more diffusely across the domain.
infographic.watch_item: Because exact simultaneous preservation of circulation and energy is not achievable except via stochastic time reparametrization, the model choice involves a structural tradeoff that must be matched carefully to the target physics.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical comparison of energy- versus circulation-preserving stochastic vortex dynamics

title: Prediction of Viscoelastic Droplet Impact Dynamics Using a Vision Transformer-Based Approach
authors: Diego A. de Aguiar, Cassio M. Oishi
abstract: Droplet impact on solid surfaces is a complex fluid dynamics problem with applications in spray cooling, inkjet printing, and pharmaceutical processing. Although numerical simulations are widely used to investigate these dynamics, their computational cost becomes significant when multiple parametric variations are considered. In this work, we investigate the use of a Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) architecture to predict the temporal evolution of viscoelastic droplets impacting solid surfaces using volume fraction fields obtained from the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. In Newtonian fluids, impact dynamics are mainly characterized by the Reynolds number $Re$, representing the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, and the Weber number $We$, representing the ratio of inertial to surface tension forces. For viscoelastic fluids, additional parameters are required to account for elastic effects, namely the solvent viscosity ratio $β$ and the Weissenberg number $Wi$, increasing simulation complexity and cost. Instead of simulating the entire droplet dynamics, the proposed approach uses only the initial 10% to 20% of the simulation to predict the remaining evolution. Depending on the prediction configuration, this strategy reduces computational cost by approximately 80% to 90% compared to full numerical simulations. The ViViT produces physically consistent predictions across different parameters and prediction horizons, successfully capturing both spreading and bouncing regimes while preserving geometric features and structural similarity. Since volume fraction fields can also be extracted from experimental videos, the proposed framework could be extended to incorporate experimental data during training, potentially improving the physical fidelity of the predicted dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: A Video Vision Transformer can learn to predict the full time evolution of viscoelastic droplet impacts from only the first 10%–20% of a simulation, cutting cost while preserving key physics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a faster surrogate for droplet-impact design in spray cooling, inkjet printing, and pharma processing where many parameter sweeps are otherwise expensive.
method: Input early-time VOF volume-fraction fields from viscoelastic droplet impact simulations.
Train a ViViT model to forecast the remaining temporal evolution of the droplet.
Use predictions across different regimes and horizons, including spreading and bouncing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports physically consistent predictions across parameter settings and horizons, with about 80%–90% reduction in computational cost versus full simulation.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is only as reliable as the training coverage of impact regimes and may need careful validation before using experimental video data or extrapolating to unseen fluid parameters.
infographic.paper_title: Prediction of Viscoelastic Droplet Impact Dynamics Using a Vision Transformer-Based Approach

title: Temperature distribution measurement on three-phase contact line in liquid nitrogen using two-color temperature-sensitive paint
authors: Shione Fujiwara, Yasuhiro Egami, Osamu Kawanami, Yu Matsuda
abstract: Cryogenic phase-change phenomena play an important role in a wide range of engineering applications, including cryogenic cooling systems, superconducting technologies, and space propulsion systems. In particular, the three-phase contact line is recognized as a key region governing evaporation and heat transfer. However, direct measurements of temperature distributions near cryogenic three-phase contact lines remain limited because conventional infrared thermography becomes increasingly difficult at extremely low temperatures. In this study, a two-color temperature-sensitive paint (2C-TSP) technique was applied to visualize the temperature field around a liquid-nitrogen three-phase contact line. A temperature-sensitive dye and a temperature-insensitive reference dye were incorporated into a single coating, enabling robust temperature measurements based on luminescence intensity ratios by compensating for changes in optical intensity caused by refraction and reflection at the liquid-gas interface. Temperature distributions were measured under three heating conditions with heat fluxes of 110, 430, and 900 W/m2. The measured temperature fields revealed a localized temperature minimum at the observed three-phase contact line, suggesting localized cooling associated with phase change. Quantitative analysis showed that the average temperature in the liquid region remained nearly constant, whereas the temperature in the gas region increased with increasing heat flux. These observations reveal a non-uniform thermal structure around the cryogenic three-phase contact line. The present results demonstrate that 2C-TSP is a promising technique for direct visualization of temperature fields around cryogenic three-phase contact lines and provides new insights into phase-change phenomena in liquid nitrogen.

infographic.key_insight: Two-color temperature-sensitive paint revealed a localized temperature minimum at the liquid-nitrogen three-phase contact line, indicating strong local cooling from phase change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a direct way to map cryogenic heat-transfer behavior at interfaces critical to cooling systems, superconducting devices, and space propulsion hardware.
method: Applied 2C-TSP with a temperature-sensitive dye plus a reference dye in one coating.
Used luminescence intensity ratios to compensate for optical distortion at the liquid-gas interface.
Measured temperature fields under heat fluxes of 110, 430, and 900 W/m² in liquid nitrogen.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a nearly constant average temperature in the liquid region, while the gas-region temperature increased with heat flux, confirming a non-uniform thermal field near the contact line.
infographic.watch_item: Accurate interpretation depends on reliable calibration and optical stability near the interface, where refraction and reflection can still affect signal quality.
infographic.paper_title: Temperature distribution measurement on three-phase contact line in liquid nitrogen using two-color temperature-sensitive paint

title: Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport
authors: Gabriel F. Barros, Rômulo M. Silva, Alvaro L. G. A. Coutinho
abstract: This chapter reviews recent advances in Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) for modeling coupled fluid flow and transport phenomena governed by the incompressible Navier-Stokes and scalar transport equations. Such systems, found in applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection, feature strong nonlinear coupling and multiscale behavior that make high-fidelity simulations computationally expensive. To address this, the chapter surveys state-of-the-art SciML methods for building efficient surrogate models, including linear reduced-order techniques based on Singular Value Decomposition (such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition) and nonlinear neural network approaches like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and $β$-Variational Autoencoders ($β$-VAEs). It first covers the authors' work combining these models with High Performance Computing strategies, including Adaptive Mesh Refinement/Coarsening (AMR/C) and scientific floating-point data compression. It then presents two new contributions: surrogate modeling of turbidity currents via PINNs, and the extraction of disentangled nonlinear modes from thermal flows using $β$-VAEs. Governing equations and representative benchmarks, including lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, illustrate these methodologies. The chapter is intentionally long, covering both the mathematical and physical foundations of coupled fluid flow and the computational aspects of state-of-the-art modeling. Overall, it demonstrates how SciML enables fast, accurate approximations of complex coupled systems within the specific data regimes and modeling assumptions considered, while substantially reducing computational cost relative to full-order simulations. Broader capabilities such as real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification remain active research directions whose feasibility depends strongly on the problem at hand.

infographic.key_insight: Scientific machine learning can replace expensive full-order simulations for coupled incompressible flow and transport by combining physics constraints with reduced-order and neural surrogate models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These surrogates can cut computational cost for applications like turbidity currents and thermal convection while preserving key flow-transport dynamics needed for design and analysis.
method: SVD-based reduced-order models, including Dynamic Mode Decomposition
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for turbidity current surrogates
β-Variational Autoencoders (β-VAEs) to extract nonlinear latent modes in thermal flows
infographic.evidence_signal: The chapter supports its review with representative benchmark problems such as lock-exchange flow and Rayleigh-Bénard convection, plus two new case studies on turbidity currents and thermal flow mode extraction.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends strongly on the specific data regime and modeling assumptions, so real-time prediction and uncertainty quantification are not guaranteed for all coupled flow problems.
infographic.paper_title: Advances in Scientific Machine Learning for Coupled Fluid Flow and Transport

title: Scaling of the minimal energy for turbulence transition in pipe flow
authors: Patrick Keuchel, Daniel Morón, Marc Avila
abstract: Predicting the transition of turbulence in pipe flow remains a fundamental problem in fluid dynamics. We use a variational approach to compute nonlinear optimal perturbations to the laminar flow at Reynolds number $Re\leq 5000$. As $Re$ increases, optimal perturbations remain structurally similar, but increasingly localize while their thickness scales as $δ_r \propto Re^{-1/3}$. They grow via the Orr mechanism, followed by a phase of strong nonlinear interaction of oblique waves and a lift-up phase. The energy gain during the Orr phase increases linearly with $Re$ and is independent of the initial perturbation energy, $E_0$. The energy gain during the oblique and lift-up phases is governed by nonlinearities and scales as $\propto Re^2$. We find that regardless of the Reynolds number, transition occurs if the energy of the perturbation exceeds a constant threshold. As a result, the minimum perturbation energy required to cause transition in pipe flow scales as $\mathcal{O}(Re^{-3})$.

infographic.key_insight: The minimum perturbation energy needed to trigger pipe-flow turbulence decreases as O(Re^-3), even though the transition pathway stays qualitatively similar and becomes more localized at higher Reynolds number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For pipe systems, this provides a predictive scaling law for robustness to disturbances, helping estimate transition risk and design flow-control strategies across Reynolds numbers.
method: Variationally computed nonlinear optimal perturbations to laminar pipe flow.
Analyzed the transition pathway through Orr growth, nonlinear oblique-wave interaction, and lift-up.
Measured how perturbation thickness, energy gain, and transition threshold scale with Reynolds number up to Re<=5000.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports computed results up to Re<=5000 showing δ_r ∝ Re^-1/3, Orr-phase gain ∝ Re, nonlinear-stage gain ∝ Re^2, and a Reynolds-independent transition threshold that implies minimal energy scales as O(Re^-3).
infographic.watch_item: The scaling is demonstrated within a finite Reynolds-number range and for optimal perturbations in an idealized pipe-flow setting, so applicability to real disturbances may require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling of the minimal energy for turbulence transition in pipe flow

title: Data assimilation of flow MRI data into RANS models with algebraic closures
authors: C. Namuroy, M. P. Juniper, P. Nair, M. Loecher, D. B. Ennis, A. Marsden
abstract: We adopt the Bayesian inference framework to solve an inverse Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) problem for the approximate posterior probability distribution of the turbulence model parameters and inlet boundary conditions of a confined turbulent jet. The data are noisy 3D flow MRI measurements of a Newtonian fluid flowing through the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) nozzle geometry. We assimilate this into RANS using two algebraic turbulence models based on the mean shear rate magnitude and the turbulence kinetic energy. We demonstrate that the inferred models are able to reconstruct the measured mean flow velocities without overfitting and we provide uncertainty estimates for the model parameters. The methodology can readily be extended to more complex RANS models, provided that they remain differentiable.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian data assimilation can calibrate simple differentiable RANS turbulence closures and inlet conditions directly from noisy 3D flow MRI while preserving predictive mean-flow reconstruction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical route to improve CFD models for complex internal flows using experimental imaging data, with quantified uncertainty for design and validation.
method: Use noisy 3D flow MRI measurements from the FDA nozzle as observational data.
Infer posterior distributions for turbulence-model parameters and inlet boundary conditions in an inverse RANS formulation.
Compare two algebraic closures: one based on mean shear-rate magnitude and one based on turbulence kinetic energy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the inferred models reconstruct the measured mean velocity field without overfitting and provide uncertainty estimates for the fitted parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on differentiable RANS closures, so extension to more complex or non-differentiable turbulence models may require additional formulation work.
infographic.paper_title: Data assimilation of flow MRI data into RANS models with algebraic closures

title: Aquatic locomotion by an elastically mounted flexible foil actuated by an oscillating force
authors: Ramon Fernandez-Feria
abstract: An analytical formulation of the fluid-structure interaction of a flexible foil driven by an oscillating force actuating on its elastically mounted leading edge, so that it can heave, pitch and deform passively with the hydrodynamic forces, is used to investigate the aquatic locomotion of a body, responsible for the whole drag and thrusted by the oscillating flexible foil. The small-amplitude theoretical model is validated with previous theoretical and experimental results for a body propelled by a rigid plate oscillating with a prescribed heaving motion and passive pitch. The inclusion of passive heave and deformation allows to expand the parametric ranges for optimal self-propulsion conditions in terms of length travelled by flapping cycle (stride length) and locomotion efficiency. In addition to the known optimal locomotion condition localized near the resonance of the torsional spring on which the foil is elastically mounted, which here is modulated by its coupling with the resonances of the translational spring and of the structural deformation of the foil, another even better local optimal locomotion condition is found near the translational spring branch of the elastic support resonance that occurs at lower stiffnesses of both springs. Unlike the local maximum of efficiency close to the natural frequency associated with the torsional spring branch, which increases with the stiffness of the foil, being the highest for a rigid foil, the larger local maximum associated with the translational spring branch increases as the stiffness of the foil decreases.

infographic.key_insight: A flexible foil elastically mounted at the leading edge can achieve better self-propulsion when passive heave and deformation are allowed, revealing an additional optimal regime near the translational spring resonance beyond the classic torsional resonance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designing flapping or bio-inspired propulsion systems should consider both spring tuning and foil flexibility, since lower stiffness can shift the best efficiency toward a distinct, higher-performing operating branch.
method: Small-amplitude analytical fluid-structure interaction model for an elastically mounted flexible foil
Leading edge driven by an oscillating force, enabling passive heave, pitch, and deformation
Model validated against prior theoretical and experimental rigid-plate results
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparison with previous theoretical and experimental results and identifies two local optima in stride length and efficiency across spring-stiffness ranges.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation is small-amplitude, so the predicted optima may not fully extend to strongly nonlinear flapping or large-deformation regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Aquatic locomotion by an elastically mounted flexible foil actuated by an oscillating force

title: Continuity equations in the Generalised Lagrangian Mean theory
authors: Vladimir A. Vladimirov
abstract: Generalised Lagrangian Mean (or Hybrid Euler-Lagrange) theory aims to describe the joint evolution of the mean flow and its perturbations. This paper considers related forms of continuity equations (CEs) and clarifies the conditions of their validity. We do not consider equations of motion; therefore, we use only exact formulae and general notions of fluid dynamics and operate only with the most general statements for CEs. The tools used are Lagrangian X, Eulerian x, averaged Eulerian x' coordinates of fluid particles, and ensemble-based averaging. The targeted forms of CEs are expressed in terms of function x(x',t). Our first step is to present the actual velocity divergence div u via div'u', where u and u' are the actual and average fluid velocities. Then we introduce three versions of exact CEs and demonstrate that each is mathematically incomplete. The third step is to restore their completeness by introducing the compatibility equations required for their validity in general fluid flows. As a basic reference, we present two versions of the McIntyre-Andrews Transformation (MAT) for CEs. The original MAT introduces an auxiliary function that satisfies an auxiliary PDE and special initial conditions. Therefore, it works for a special class of fluid flows. The presented generalisation of MAT makes CEs applicable to arbitrary fluid motion. Both versions require compatibility equations, which we compare with ours. Finally, we consider average flows with small perturbations, thereby linking our exposition to the classical GLM theory.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that several commonly used continuity equations in Generalised Lagrangian Mean theory are mathematically incomplete unless extra compatibility conditions are added.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This clarifies when GLM-style mean-flow models can be trusted in turbulent flow analysis and how to extend them to arbitrary fluid motion.
method: Derives the actual velocity divergence in terms of averaged Eulerian quantities
Formulates three exact continuity-equation variants and identifies what is missing in each
Restores validity by introducing compatibility equations and comparing them with McIntyre-Andrews Transformations
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a theory/derivation study based on exact formulae and general fluid-dynamic statements rather than numerical experiments or datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The original MAT applies only under special flow assumptions, so implementations must enforce the required auxiliary PDE and compatibility conditions before using these continuity forms.
infographic.paper_title: Continuity equations in the Generalised Lagrangian Mean theory

title: Eulerian Lagrangian relations in decaying two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes fluids across initial vorticity packing and Reynolds number
authors: Snehanshu Maiti, Rajaraman Ganesh
abstract: Recent studies Vorticity packing effects on long time turbulent transport in decaying two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes fluids, Phys. Fluids 38, 045159 (2026) demonstrated that, at a fixed high Reynolds number (Re), the initial vorticity packing fraction (VPF) governs the coupled Eulerian flow evolution and Lagrangian tracer particle transport in decaying two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes fluids, revealing a strong Eulerian Lagrangian relationship during the nonequilibrium inverse cascade regime and a direct Eulerian Lagrangian correspondence in the late time coherent vortex quasi equilibrium regime, wherein increasing VPF drives transitions from point vortex to patch vortex equilibria and from subdiffusive to superdiffusive transport. In the present work, we investigate how these Eulerian Lagrangian connections evolve across a broad (VPF, Re) parameter space. The results show that the Eulerian Lagrangian relationship remains largely preserved during the nonequilibrium inverse-cascade regime, where transport increases systematically with VPF and remains primarily controlled by VPF despite secondary Re dependent oscillatory modulation. In contrast, the late-time coherent-vortex quasi-equilibrium regime exhibits Eulerian statistical equilibria that remain largely insensitive to Re, while the corresponding tracer-particle transport displays a strong Re dependence characterized by strong oscillatory and nonmonotonic variations across the (VPF, Re) parameter space, substantially weakening the VPF-ordered transport hierarchy observed in the inverse-cascade regime. Consequently, for the parameter range, spatial resolutions, and integration times explored in the present study, the direct Eulerian Lagrangian correspondence identified at fixed high Re is not universally maintained across the broader (VPF, Re) parameter space.

infographic.key_insight: Initial vorticity packing fraction (VPF) remains the main driver of Eulerian–Lagrangian coupling in the inverse-cascade regime, but at late times and across broader Reynolds numbers the tracer-transport order becomes strongly Re-dependent and the simple correspondence breaks down.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For 2D decaying Navier–Stokes systems, both initial vortex packing and Reynolds number must be accounted for when predicting mixing, transport, and coherence in reduced-order models or flow-control studies.
method: Parameter sweep over initial vorticity packing fraction (VPF) and Reynolds number (Re) in decaying 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes flows.
Compare Eulerian flow statistics with Lagrangian tracer-particle transport across nonequilibrium inverse-cascade and late-time coherent-vortex regimes.
Assess whether transport ordering by VPF persists or weakens as Re varies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports systematic transport increase with VPF in the inverse-cascade regime, but strong oscillatory and nonmonotonic Re dependence in the late-time regime, based on the explored (VPF, Re) parameter space, resolutions, and integration times.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is limited to the parameter range, spatial resolutions, and simulation times studied, so the observed breakdown of direct Eulerian–Lagrangian correspondence may not generalize outside that domain.
infographic.paper_title: Eulerian Lagrangian relations in decaying two dimensional incompressible Navier Stokes fluids across initial vorticity packing and Reynolds number

title: Scaling patch analysis of turbulent kinetic energy budget equation in wall-bounded flows
authors: Tie Wei, Zhaorui Li, Sergio Pirozzoli
abstract: The scaling patch approach is applied to analyze the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budget equation in wall-bounded turbulent flows. The balance of the TKE equation is divided into several distinct regions, or scaling patches, each characterized by a dominant balance among the governing terms and its own appropriate scaling parameters. In the near-wall viscous sublayer, the TKE balance is primarily between viscous diffusion and dissipation, and the characteristic scales are set by the kinematic viscosity and the wall dissipation rate. The thickness of this sublayer is on the order of the Kolmogorov length scale. Moving away from the wall, the peak TKE production provides a natural reference scale for the inner layer, yielding the traditional inner scaling. Grouping the viscous diffusion and dissipation terms in the inner layer enhances the collapse across different Reynolds numbers. In the outer region, Prandtl's mixing-length model is used to derive a characteristic scale for TKE production. A new meso-scaling is further introduced to describe the intermediate region, ensuring a smooth transition between the inner and outer layers. The scaling patch framework offers a unified interpretation of the structure and scaling behavior of the TKE budget across all regions of wall-bounded turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: The paper partitions the turbulent kinetic energy budget in wall-bounded flows into distinct scaling patches, each governed by a different dominant balance and scaling law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This unified patch-based scaling can improve interpretation and modeling of near-wall, intermediate, and outer-layer turbulence across Reynolds numbers.
method: Apply scaling-patch analysis to the TKE budget equation in wall-bounded turbulence.
Use viscous diffusion–dissipation balance to define the near-wall sublayer and Kolmogorov-length thickness.
Introduce inner, meso, and outer scalings using peak TKE production and Prandtl mixing-length ideas.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical framework validated by comparing the TKE budget structure across wall-bounded-flow regions and Reynolds numbers, emphasizing improved collapse under the proposed scalings.
infographic.watch_item: The patch boundaries and scaling choices may be flow-regime dependent, so extending the framework to other wall-bounded configurations may require careful recalibration.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling patch analysis of turbulent kinetic energy budget equation in wall-bounded flows

title: Turbulence Physics Governs a Scaling Law for the Machine-Learning Predictability Ceiling in Chaotic Flow
authors: Jiashun Guan, Haoyang Hu, Yunxiao Ren, Michael S. Triantafyllou, Dixia Fan
abstract: For centuries, the intrinsic chaos of unsteady fluid motion has stood as a formidable barrier to long-term forecasting. While machine learning (ML) has recently emerged as a transformative paradigm for predicting flow evolution, it encounters a pervasive yet unexplained "performance wall": an inevitable deterioration in accuracy as the forecast horizon extends. Here, we demonstrate that this deterioration is not a deficiency of model architecture, no matter how state-of-the-art, but a fundamental constraint imposed by the underlying system, which can be understood through turbulence theory established decades ago. In the setting of bluff body flow, a canonical phenomenon for spatiotemporal complexity in fluid mechanics, we reveal a scaling law governing the deterioration of ML predictability, derived from a Kolmogorov-inspired framework and validated through high-fidelity simulations. Our findings establish a closed loop between the predictability ceiling and its interpretation, bridging the gap between transparent physical theories and modern black-box inference. More broadly, this work provides a theoretical compass for constructing trustworthy ML in complex dynamical systems across the physical sciences.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learning forecasts of chaotic bluff-body flow hit a physics-based predictability ceiling that scales with turbulence theory, not just model quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives engineers a principled way to estimate when ML flow prediction will become unreliable and to design forecasting horizons around intrinsic fluid-dynamics limits.
method: Derived a scaling law for ML forecast deterioration using a Kolmogorov-inspired turbulence framework.
Tested the law on bluff-body flow, a canonical spatiotemporally chaotic fluid system.
Validated the prediction against high-fidelity simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on high-fidelity simulations of bluff-body flow, linking forecast degradation to an analytically derived scaling law.
infographic.watch_item: The result is established for bluff-body flow, so transfer to other flow regimes or sensor/ML setups may require re-validation of the scaling law.
infographic.paper_title: Turbulence Physics Governs a Scaling Law for the Machine-Learning Predictability Ceiling in Chaotic Flow

title: How is the free surface influence transported in turbulent open channel flows?
authors: Yoshiyuki Sakai, Christian Bauer
abstract: We investigate how the influence of a free surface is transported in turbulent open channel flow by analysing matched open- and closed-channel direct numerical simulations up to $Re_\mathrmτ \approx 900$ in a domain large enough to accommodate very-large-scale motions (VLSMs). The turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) budget shows that the surface influence is communicated primarily through transport terms. Near the free surface, pressure transport supplies energy towards the interface, whereas turbulent transport and dissipation are reduced; the resulting energy surplus is exported away from the surface predominantly by viscous diffusion. The near-surface budget terms do not exhibit a single universal similarity scaling: viscous diffusion is organised over the near-surface viscous scale $\ell_\mathrm{V}$, dissipation over the Kolmogorov sublayer scale $\ell_\mathrm{K}$, and pressure-related terms require the mixed velocity scale $u_\mathrm{b} u_\mathrmτ^2 /h$. The pressure-strain redistribution further reveals outer-inner coupling: although intense pressure-strain events remain small-scale, their magnitude and directional bias are organised by low-velocity VLSM streaks. The free-surface influence is therefore best understood as a coupled multi-scale process involving local kinematic constraints, Reynolds-number-dependent surface layers, and outer-layer coherent motions.

infographic.key_insight: Free-surface effects in turbulent open-channel flow are transported mainly by pressure-related and viscous transport terms, and they couple near-wall scales with outer-layer very-large-scale motions rather than following one universal scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For open-channel and hydraulic design, this means surface-driven momentum and energy exchange can influence near-surface mixing, turbulence models, and boundary-condition assumptions across multiple scales.
method: Matched open- and closed-channel DNS up to Re_tau ≈ 900
Compared turbulent kinetic energy budget terms near the free surface
Examined pressure-strain redistribution and scale organization using VLSM-resolving domains
infographic.evidence_signal: The analysis uses direct numerical simulations with matched configurations and a domain large enough to capture very-large-scale motions, enabling term-by-term comparison of near-surface TKE budgets.
infographic.watch_item: The reported near-surface scaling is not universal, so applying a single wall-law or one-scale surface model may miss Reynolds-number-dependent and outer-layer coupling effects.
infographic.paper_title: How is the free surface influence transported in turbulent open channel flows?

title: Effects of mean flow skew on turbulent shear layers. Part I. Numerical investigation
authors: Vedant Kumar, Dipendra Gupta, Gregory Paul Bewley, Johan Larsson
abstract: Skewed turbulent shear layers, formed by the interaction between two non-aligned turbulent boundary layers, are investigated using high-fidelity large eddy simulations in a temporally evolving framework. It is argued that a skewed shear layer of this form should be viewed, in the long-time limit, in a rotated reference frame as the superposition of a standard planar shear layer and an orthogonal jet-like component that decays in time. The skewed shear layer is found to have reduced vertical integral length scale, and the coherent pressure rollers characteristic of shear layers undergo transient realignment towards the direction orthogonal to mean shear, consistent with the long-time limiting planar shear layer. Numerical experiments using fictitious test cases indicate that these effects are primarily driven through misalignment in the mean flow, and that the two orthogonal flow components in the mean shear frame are only weakly coupled.

infographic.key_insight: A mean-flow-skewed turbulent shear layer behaves like a standard planar shear layer plus a decaying orthogonal jet-like component, with coherent structures gradually reorienting toward the planar-shear direction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This implies that misalignment in boundary-layer interactions can materially change mixing, length scales, and coherent-structure dynamics in turbulence modeling and flow-control design.
method: High-fidelity large eddy simulations of a temporally evolving skewed shear layer
Rotated-frame interpretation of the flow into shear-aligned and orthogonal components
Fictitious test cases to isolate the role of mean-flow misalignment
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports LES-based numerical evidence showing reduced vertical integral length scale and transient roller realignment, with weak coupling between the two orthogonal mean-flow components.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are based on temporally evolving numerical cases, so applying them directly to spatially developing or strongly three-dimensional flows may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of mean flow skew on turbulent shear layers. Part I. Numerical investigation

title: A Methodology to Quantify Interscale Energy Transfer at Solid Boundaries
authors: Lennard Miller
abstract: Far away from solid boundaries, energy can be transferred between different flow scales due to the non-linear self-advection of velocity. This energy transfer can be quantified using well-established Fourier diagnostics or filtering methods. However, these diagnostic tools fail to provide a physical representation of the linear energy transfer that may occur during the formation of oceanic boundary layers or Rossby wave reflections. In this document, I outline a novel filtering methodology that is able to quantify this linear energy transfer by combining coarse-graining with volume-penalization. Its utility is illustrated by quantifying the down-scale energy transfer occuring during a Rossby wave reflection off a western boundary. The conceptual framework developed here is thought to be broadly applicable to the study of multi-scale energetics of bounded geophysical fluid flows.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a filtering-based methodology that combines coarse-graining with volume penalization to quantify interscale energy transfer near solid boundaries, where standard Fourier or filtering diagnostics are insufficient.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical tool for analyzing boundary-layer energetics and wave–boundary interactions in geophysical and engineering flows with walls or immersed solids.
method: Combine coarse-graining with volume-penalization to preserve a physical representation of boundary effects.
Use the resulting filter to quantify linear energy transfer at solid boundaries.
Apply the framework to Rossby wave reflection to measure down-scale transfer at a western boundary.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an illustrative application to Rossby wave reflection off a western boundary, demonstrating the method on a bounded geophysical flow case.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is presented as a novel framework and its broader accuracy and robustness likely depend on careful implementation for different boundary geometries and flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: A Methodology to Quantify Interscale Energy Transfer at Solid Boundaries

title: Non-monotonic variations in pressure drop and chaos in viscoelastic fluid flows through an ordered microporous medium
authors: A. Chauhan, C. Sasmal
abstract: Several recent experimental studies have revealed non-monotonic variations in elastic turbulence-induced chaotic flow behaviour and pressure drop during the flow of viscoelastic fluids through a microporous medium. The present numerical study aims to investigate and hypothesise about the physical mechanisms governing these complex flow behaviours in an ordered microporous medium consisting of cylindrical micropillars arranged in a staggered configuration. We propose that birefringent strands of high elastic stress, generated by the stretching and alignment of polymer molecules within the porous structure, play the dominant role in controlling the non-monotonic variations in chaos and pressure drop. At low Weissenberg numbers, these stress strands develop gradually, mainly downstream of the micropillars, whereas beyond a critical Weissenberg number, they begin to fluctuate strongly, leading to chaotic flow dynamics. However, at even higher Weissenberg numbers, the strands become larger and stronger, eventually interconnecting between neighbouring micropillars, causing the flow to reorganise into a nearly steady, ordered state similar to that observed at low Weissenberg numbers. On the other hand, the pressure drop in the system consists of a mean contribution, obtained from statistically stationary flow quantities, and a fluctuating contribution. While the mean component increases monotonically with the Weissenberg number, the fluctuating component varies non-monotonically, leading to a similar trend in the total pressure drop. Moreover, the non-monotonic chaotic behaviour strongly depends on the solid volume fraction of the porous medium, which alters both the critical Weissenberg number for instability onset and the range over which the non-monotonic behaviour persists.

infographic.key_insight: In ordered microporous viscoelastic flow, elastic stress strands first trigger chaos, then can reorganize into a more ordered state at higher Weissenberg numbers, producing non-monotonic chaos and pressure-drop trends.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designing porous media and operating conditions around the critical Weissenberg number and solid volume fraction could help control drag, flow stability, and process performance in polymer-processing and filtration systems.
method: Numerical study of viscoelastic flow through a staggered array of cylindrical micropillars.
Tracks birefringent high-stress strands, flow chaos, and pressure-drop components versus Weissenberg number.
Examines how changing solid volume fraction shifts instability onset and the non-monotonic regime.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports statistically stationary flow quantities for the mean pressure drop and identifies a fluctuating contribution that varies non-monotonically with Weissenberg number, alongside a critical instability threshold.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are based on an ordered microporous geometry, so behavior may differ in disordered media or under different constitutive models and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Non-monotonic variations in pressure drop and chaos in viscoelastic fluid flows through an ordered microporous medium

title: Bi-stable Nonlinear Energy Sinks (BNESs) for Response Mitigation and Drag Reduction of Subsea Cables Undergoing Vortex-induced Vibrations
authors: Anargyros Michaloliakos, Ryan Davies, Matthew Hall, Alexander F. Vakakis
abstract: A methodology for passive mitigation of vortex-induced vibrations (VIVs) in subsea dynamic power cables is developed using optimized, strongly nonlinear bi-stable mass-spring-damper attachments, termed bi-stable nonlinear energy sinks (BNESs), within the open-source MoorDyn library. A fully three-dimensional time-domain framework captures cable dynamics, Morison-type hydrodynamic forcing, nonlinear vibration-mitigation mechanisms, and spatially and temporally varying currents. The BNESs are consistently integrated into the cable model, allowing treatment of highly non-stationary VIVs. A data-driven optimization study samples the BNES design space across multiple current profiles and shows that properly tuned configurations substantially reduce peak-to-peak cable vibration amplitudes. The BNESs also produce significant and robust reductions in cumulative VIV-induced energy intake from the surrounding flow and in drag energy. To the authors' knowledge, passive nonlinear attachments are shown for the first time to reduce both energy intake and drag amplification in a subsea cable, with potential benefits for short- and long-term fatigue. Time-frequency wavelet analysis reveals targeted nonlinear energy transfers and scattering from dominant high-amplitude, low-frequency cable modes to lower-amplitude, higher-frequency modes. This modal redistribution promotes rapid dissipation through hydrodynamic damping and internal structural losses, explaining the simultaneous reductions in vibration amplitude and cumulative energy intake. The results demonstrate that BNESs can provide effective and robust VIV mitigation for subsea power cables under realistic unsteady operating conditions and motivate future studies involving combined current-wave loading, platform-induced motion, and fatigue-life assessment.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized bi-stable nonlinear energy sinks passively redirect vortex-induced vibration energy in subsea cables into higher-frequency, more easily dissipated motions, reducing both vibration and drag.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a passive, retrofit-friendly way to improve subsea cable durability and fatigue life under realistic unsteady currents.
method: Integrated BNES attachments into the open-source MoorDyn cable model
Simulated fully 3D time-domain cable dynamics with Morison-type hydrodynamic forcing and varying currents
Used data-driven optimization across multiple current profiles to tune BNES parameters
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the sampled design space, well-tuned BNES configurations consistently reduced peak-to-peak vibration amplitudes, cumulative VIV energy intake, and drag energy.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on careful tuning and validation under broader load cases such as combined waves, platform motion, and long-term fatigue conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Bi-stable Nonlinear Energy Sinks (BNESs) for Response Mitigation and Drag Reduction of Subsea Cables Undergoing Vortex-induced Vibrations
